title: Robert Bosch Moves His Stuttgart Works to an Eight-Hour Day, 1906
dek: After a trial of two shifts, Bosch cut the working day to eight hours from 1 August 1906, and rivals called him the red Bosch.

story.event: Introducing the eight-hour working day at the Stuttgart works
story.summary: After trying a two-shift system in 1905, Robert Bosch introduced the eight-hour day at his Stuttgart works from 1 August 1906, when most comparable German firms worked far longer weeks. Competitors attacked him for it and he became known as 'the red Bosch'; he argued that rested workers produced better work. Later rationalisation and piece-rate disputes led to a strike that shut the works in the summer of 1913.
paragraphs: From 1 August 1906, the working day at Robert Bosch's works in Stuttgart was eight hours. Bosch, then 44, had opened his workshop for precision mechanics in the city in 1886 with 10,000 marks inherited from his father. He knew how fragile it could be: in the slump of 1892 he had let go all but two of his 24 employees. Since 1902 his high-voltage magneto had made the firm an international supplier, and by the company's own account an American newspaper advertisement in 1906 brought a million dollars of orders and doubled sales within a year.

The works had kept a nine-hour day since 1894. In 1905, as the business grew, Bosch tried running it in two shifts. The results were good, and so he cut the day to eight hours, a 48-hour week. It was a long way from the norm. As late as 1910, more than half of comparable firms still worked 57 to 60 hours a week, and nearly a third worked more. Competitors attacked him for the shorter day, and among industrialists he became known as der rote Bosch, the red Bosch.

He did not present it as charity. He argued that it was better, for workers and for the country, to get the highest output from a shorter working time, and that someone with longer to recover worked more gladly and kept his mind on the job. Skilled workers were scarce, and good conditions were meant to hold on to them. He refused company welfare schemes, which he thought bred dependence, and paid above-average wages instead.

The shorter day did not end conflict. As the works moved to mass production, frequent changes to piece rates drew Bosch into a dispute with the metalworkers' union, and after two toolmakers were dismissed on 31 May 1913, a mass strike led to the works being shut from early June to mid-July. It strained his good relations with the unions for some time. Bosch later said it had not always been easy to keep to the middle way between the entrepreneur who must hold his ground and the socially minded businessman. In 1941 he still called the eight-hour model the best for preserving people's working strength.

quote.text: In striving for others, avoid fame. In striving for self, avoid disgrace. Pursue a middle course. Thus you will keep a sound body, and a sound mind, fulfil your duties, and work out your allotted span.
quote.source_title: Chuang Tzŭ: Mystic, Moralist, and Social Reformer, tr. Herbert A. Giles, Project Gutenberg eBook #59709
quote.connection: Bosch described his own position as a middle way between the businessman who must survive and the one who thinks of his workers. Zhuangzi sets the middle course in a person's own life, as the way to keep body and mind sound while still fulfilling one's duties.

reflection: Bosch did not treat the shorter day as a reward for good work. He treated it as part of how good work gets made: people with time to recover keep their minds on the job. He also found that a fair policy does not settle every dispute.

When you are building something, the first hours to go are usually your own evenings, and the last person whose working day you count is yourself. If the argument held for a workshop full of precision mechanics, it may hold for you too. Your attention is the tool that has to last.
invitation: Choose a time to stop work tonight and tell one person at home what it is. When it comes, stop, even if the last task is not finished.

cross_checks.claim: Bosch introduced the eight-hour day at his works in 1906 (from 1 August 1906, per the Bosch-Archiv study)
He was among the first employers in Germany to do so
He was known as 'der rote Bosch' (the red Bosch)
He paid above-average wages and refused works welfare schemes
A strike in 1913 strained his relations with the unions

research_notes: Date: most sources give only 1906; Zimmermann's study (based on the Bosch-Archiv and citing the company's 2011 history) gives 1 August 1906 and says a two-shift system had been tested in 1905. The free Saturday afternoon is dated 1908 in Heuss's NDB article and 1910 in Zimmermann (citing Herdt and Heuss's biography); the story does not mention it. Hours: the 1910 comparison (54 per cent of comparable firms at 57-60 hours, 32 per cent at over 60 to 72) is Zimmermann citing Prinzing, so the story says 'as late as 1910' rather than claiming it for 1906. Bosch's arguments for shorter hours and his remark on the middle way are German quotations reproduced in Zimmermann (from Geißel's works-council history and the company's jubilee volume); they are paraphrased, not quoted, because no English original exists. The 1941 phrase is from a Reichssender Stuttgart interview, quoted by Zimmermann, and is also paraphrased. The million-dollar order figure for the 1906 US advertisement is the company's own claim and is attributed to it. The wages line ('I don't pay good wages because I have a lot of money...') appears on Bosch's history site but its original source is not given, so it was left out. The 1913 strike: Heuss calls it 'senseless', which is the authorised biographer's judgement; the story does not assign blame and gives only the sequence of events from Zimmermann. Age: born 23 September 1861 (LeMO, Robert Bosch Stiftung), so 44 in August 1906. Funding: Heuss states the firm grew without outside capital apart from an American loan after the 1920s inflation, hence 'bootstrapped'.
